issues.title: Roads / Cardboard Construction Toys / Quick fix for leaks
issues.html:
Projective road cards

This year I stayed at an Airbnb owned by a therapist and discovered Roads, a deck of 67 projective cards that therapists use to help clients picture where they are in life and where they want to go. Each card shows an illustrated path or road, and there are many ways to use them. You can pick one for a new direction you’d like to take, or lay out several to map your journey from where you are now to where you hope to be. Either way, the images start speaking for your inner landscape. It’s made for therapy, but I bought a deck for my own solo reflection. While searching for it, I also found Play Therapy Supply, which seems like a great source for introspective tools even if you’re not a play therapist. — CD

Cardboard Construction Toys

In my experience the greatest toys for kids are large sheets of cardboard from recycled oversized boxes. It’s free. With the addition of a few plastic screws you or the kids can make endless forts, fantasy structures and even costumes by cobbling the cardboard together. The screws I use have a hex head that fits a socket driver or screwdriver. You make a hole with an awl and then hand drive the screw in. Easy and safe for kids to do. The screws are easy to extract and re-use in the next project. A set of Kizzikids 160 screws with 2 drivers ($20) will have more pieces than you’ll ever need – but perfect for a school or camp. Or, if you have a 3D printer you can print Cardboard Fasteners yourself. — KK

Quick fix for leaks

I used Iron Grip self-fusing silicone tape to temporarily patch a leaky hose on my car. To activate it, stretch the tape, then wrap it tightly around a leaky pipe, hose, or wire. It’s great to have some around for plumbing leaks when they happen. You can also wrap it around tool handles for a more comfortable grip. I used the Iron Grip brand, but many other brands are available, and I imagine they’re all pretty much the same. — MF

Charity Navigator

Tis the season to remember the power of philanthropy. Small gifts, well aimed, can make significant impacts. When we are evaluating new-to-us charitable orgs, we use Charity Navigator to assess their reputation, how responsible and transparent they are with their finances. If you are trying to compare global health programs in terms of how many lives are saved or improved per dollar, try GiveWell. If you want to improve the world by supporting art, do your own thing, but do it generously. There are few pleasures as lasting as giving. — KK

Natural hazards by address

If you live in California, MyHazards is a good place to find out which natural hazards you're most susceptible to. Type in your address, city, or ZIP code, and it shows whether you're near earthquake, flood, fire, or tsunami risk, along with practical steps to prepare for each one. I looked up my own address because of all the El Niño talk and learned I'm not in a flood zone, but I am in an earthquake liquefaction zone. It's free and run by the state's Office of Emergency Services. — CD

1,700 free university courses

The Open Culture website maintains a directory of about 1,700 free online courses from top universities like Yale, MIT, Harvard, and Oxford. They are organized by category. Courses include literature, history, philosophy, religion, computer science, physics, biology, economics, psychology, engineering, and more. The courses are offered in audio, video, and text, and none of them require signing up or payment. It’s like a free university you can dip into anytime you want, or a good way to try out a subject before enrolling in a class. Open Culture also has free movies, ebooks, and art images. — MF

issues.title: Design Prompts / RetroCodex / Sunshine Atlas
issues.html:
Design Prompts

This year I manufactured Design Prompts, a box of 110 double-sided cards to help creative people get unstuck. They are inspired by Brian Eno’s Oblique Strategies, but the 216 prompts here are all my own, and more general purpose. And the beautiful box I made for them is much easier to use and store. Magnetic cover, upright stance. Draw a card at random and try what it suggests: “Find the third side” or “Change what you’re optimizing.” Hundreds more. It’s for artists, writers, designers, makers, inventors, and other innovators. Limited edition: only 400 copies, available on Amazon. I use mine all the time. — KK

Update your outdated facts

When you’re young, you learn facts about the world that are later debunked or revised. If you’re curious to see what has changed since you graduated from high school, check out RetroCodex. I learned that Tyrannosaurus rex probably had lips that covered its teeth, that adults can indeed grow new brain cells, that the appendix might actually have a purpose, and that eating eggs won’t raise your blood cholesterol. It also corrected many other facts I was taught the opposite of. It’s a fun way to update your out-of-date mental factbook. — MF

Where the sun is

I don’t like to travel during the winter, but I do like fantasizing about where I could go that’s warm and sunny, so I think Sunshine Atlas is a really cool idea. Pick a month, and the map ranks places around the world by how warm, dry, and sunny they tend to be. It has more parameters and filters than I need, but as a way to chase the sun, it works. Every destination has its own airport, so everything on the map is somewhere you can actually fly. — CD

Posca pens for painting rocks

Kevin has already recommended Posca markers here, but I want to add my own endorsement of these water-based acrylic paint pens. I like to paint on small rocks and have experimented with all kinds of acrylics and gouaches. But as soon as I tried Posca pens, I realized they are superior to a paintbrush. The colors are opaque and vibrant, and I have much more control with a pen nib than with a brush. They work on many surfaces besides rocks, too, including wood, glass, metal, ceramic, and fabric. They come in a range of tip sizes, from extra-fine to broad. — MF

Optimistic adventures

There are a lot of folks vlogging their adventures on YouTube, and you get to travel with them vicariously. Only a few are people I would actually want to spend time with. One guy who makes me happy is Matt Spears. He does stunts like riding a jet ski 1,000 miles to Alaska, or seeing how far he can get on a motorcycle chopper bought on Amazon, and so forth. Things are constantly falling apart, but he is constantly chipper, upbeat, confident, excited, enthusiastic, and his optimism is contagious. I’ll tag along wherever he wants to go. — KK

Live guided imagery journey

A while back I recommended the Pearl Dive, a 30-minute guided imagery journey I listen to whenever I feel confusion or resistance in my body. Dr. Rosalind Watts created it to prepare participants for a clinical trial of psilocybin for depression. It guides you out of your thoughts and down into your body, where buried emotions and desires are waiting. I always discover something new, and when I stay with what feels uncomfortable, it so often becomes a pearl of insight. I’m sharing it again because in a few days Dr. Watts is leading the dive live in a free Zoom session (no psychedelics involved), open to anyone preparing to explore altered states or simply wanting to go deeper into their own experience. Full disclosure, I’m a facilitator with her community, ACER Integration, but being guided through this practice by its creator, for free and in community, feels like a rare gift. The session is Wednesday, November 11, from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. UK time. You can learn more and register for free here. — CD

issues.title: Retro Recomendo: Destinations Vol. 2
issues.html:
Here’s a link to our first Destinations issue.

Our subscriber base has grown so much since we first started ten years ago that most of you have missed all our earliest recommendations. The best of these are still valid and useful, so we’re trying out something new — Retro Recomendo. Once every 6 weeks, we’ll send out a throwback issue of evergreen recommendations focused on one theme from the past 10 years.


Walk across Bali

I just completed a six-day walk across the island of Bali. We carried only day packs and our luggage was forwarded each day. We walked roughly 77 km from Ubud, up to the volcanoes in the center of the island, and then finished on the north coast. We had two guides to lead the way through the rice terraces, and we slept in local villages, Balinese style along the way. I highly recommend the organizers, who charge only $500 for the whole trip, including all the vegetarian meals along the way. This is miles off the tourist, or even backpacker, tracks. The hosts, Astungkara Way, also offer a 10-day version which goes coast to coast. — KK

Walkable Neighborhoods map

Close.city is an interactive map designed to help you find neighborhoods in the United States that are within a short walking distance of amenities like supermarkets, public transportation, cafes, co-working spaces, bookstores, and other facilities. It's useful when searching for a hotel, Airbnb, or apartment that's near the kinds of places that are important to you — MF

Find a Moon Tree near you

I didn’t know about the tree seeds that flew around the Moon in 1971 and were planted upon return until I read this article in The Atlantic: We Almost Forgot About the Moon Trees. All of the locations of these Moon Trees are kept here and up-to-date, including the ones no longer alive. Visiting as many of these trees as possible is now on my travel bucket list. — CD

Offbeat attractions guide

Whenever I travel I search for my destination at the Atlas Obscura website. It will yield dozens of very obscure, very offbeat attractions in the area. How else can you find a nearby museum of parasites, or trail of doll heads, or a restaurant of robots, underground tunnels, or a store for time travel? — KK

360-degree videos from around the world

Visit AirPano to watch 360 videos of beautiful places on Earth, from Tokyo’s Shibuya Scramble pedestrian crossing (the busiest in the world), to a village of the Warao Indigenous people on the Orinoco River in Venezuela. My travel bucket list grew after watching some of these videos. — MF

Calendar of festivals

I try to coordinate my travel to exotic places with local festivals that occur at the same time. Trouble is, there’s been no easy way to find out which festivals are happening where. For example many traditional celebrations run on a lunar cycle. So I built a calendar that will show me all the festivals in Asia that are happening on a particular day. Or I can look at the map and see what festivals occur nearby and when. My site is called Festivo. It provides the local festivals of Asia—which are crammed with color, costumes, and traditions—in calendar format. It’s open and free to all, no ads. If enough people (besides myself) find it useful I will expand it to Europe, Africa, and the rest of the world. — KK
